# SkillPrivus: Uncovering PRIV acy of US e Harms in Agentic Skills
###### Abstract
Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users’ files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. We study these potential privacy-of-use harms through SkillPrivus, a static audit framework that analyzes skills before installation without executing them. SkillPrivus extracts data operations from code and natural-language instructions, grounds them in source evidence, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess their appropriateness.
Applied to 726 real skills from public marketplaces, 563 of which handle personal data, SkillPrivus flags at least one potential violation in 307 of these skills (54.5%), and its judgments agree with three blind human annotators on 83.2% (κ=0.35) of resolvable moves.
To tackle this, we design SkillPrivus, a static privacy audit framework that analyzes skills without executing them. It screens for personal-data handling, decomposes code and instructions into source-grounded *data moves*, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess each move against the skill’s stated purpose and contextual norms. Potential privacy harms are classified using Solove’s taxonomy (Solove, 2006), which we extend with *inference* to capture newly derived sensitive attributes.
We apply SkillPrivus to 726 skills in the wild collected from popular public marketplaces and official repositories, of which 563 handle privacy-relevant data, SkillPrivus flags at least one potential violation in 307 of them, which is 54.5% of the privacy-relevant skills.

# Privacy audit flags over half of AI agent skills handling personal data
A static check of 563 public AI assistant add-ons found that 307 may use people's data beyond what their descriptions say. It also flagged skills that NVIDIA's security scanner had already passed. The study is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

The authors built a tool, SkillPrivus, that reads a skill's code and instruction files without running it. It breaks the skill into individual data operations, such as reading, saving, sending or inferring information. Each operation is pinned to the exact line of source it comes from.

The authors collected 726 skills from public marketplaces, including ClawHub and SkillsMP, plus Anthropic's and NVIDIA's official collections. After setting aside skills with no personal data and some that failed analysis, 563 remained. The tool, run on the open-weight model gpt-oss-120b, flagged at least one potential violation in 307 of them, about 55%.

## The study

Title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills

Authors: Boyin Tan, Jiadong Zhang, Xiaosong Ma, Chun Jason Xue, Xiaowei Huang, Youcheng Sun

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
Abstract
Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

SkillPrivus finds privacy risks in 307 of 563 AI agent skills

The tool found a possible violation in 54.5 percent of the skills that use personal data, and it did this before installation.
Researchers made SkillPrivus, a tool that reads an agent skill before installation and does not operate it. A skill is a set of instructions and code that gives an AI assistant new functions. The team tested 726 skills from open marketplaces. Of 563 skills that use personal data, 307 had at least 1 possible privacy violation.

How it works

SkillPrivus gets data operations from the code and from the text instructions. It connects each one to its position in the source. Then it checks if the use of the data is correct for its context.

The numbers

The tool found a possible violation in 54.5 percent of the 563 skills. Its results agree with 3 blind human annotators in 83.2 percent of the items that have a clear answer.

What is not known

The marked items are possible violations, not shown damage. The paper does not tell how many skills cause damage in use. The behaviors are sensitive inferences, use of data for more than the task of the skill, and disclosure to other recipients.

Insight: Skills can break privacy while they do their task

The paper tells that the damage comes from the functions that skills have, not from attacks. An earlier tool makes open records of agent work, and one more tool lets agents read software on the machine of the user. This reads as a race: tools that record agents and give them more functions move at a higher speed than checks of the data use of skills. A check before installation can become a gate.
Why it made the cut
For teams that let staff install agent skills: make a list of the skills with access to files and accounts, and examine the ones that use personal data first.

###### Abstract

Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users’ files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. We study these potential privacy-of-use harms through SkillPrivus , a static audit framework that analyzes skills before installation without executing them. SkillPrivus extracts data operations from code and natural-language instructions, grounds them in source evidence, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess their appropriateness. Applied to 726 real skills from public marketplaces, 563 of which handle personal data, SkillPrivus flags at least one potential violation in 307 of these skills (54.5%), and its judgments agree with three blind human annotators on 83.2% ( $\kappa=0.35$ ) of resolvable moves. The flagged behaviors include sensitive inferences, information use beyond the stated task, and disclosures to unexpected recipients, suggesting that privacy harms can arise from ordinary skill functionality.

SkillPrivus finds privacy risks in 307 of 563 AI agent skills

The tool found a possible violation in 54.5 percent of the skills that use personal data, and it did this before installation.
Researchers made SkillPrivus, a tool that reads an agent skill before installation and does not operate it. A skill is a set of instructions and code that gives an AI assistant new functions. The team tested 726 skills from open marketplaces. Of 563 skills that use personal data, 307 had at least 1 possible privacy violation.

How it works

SkillPrivus gets data operations from the code and from the text instructions. It connects each one to its position in the source. Then it checks if the use of the data is correct for its context.

The numbers

The tool found a possible violation in 54.5 percent of the 563 skills. Its results agree with 3 blind human annotators in 83.2 percent of the items that have a clear answer.

What is not known

The marked items are possible violations, not shown damage. The paper does not tell how many skills cause damage in use. The behaviors are sensitive inferences, use of data for more than the task of the skill, and disclosure to other recipients.

Insight: Skills can break privacy while they do their task

The paper tells that the damage comes from the functions that skills have, not from attacks. An earlier tool makes open records of agent work, and one more tool lets agents read software on the machine of the user. This reads as a race: tools that record agents and give them more functions move at a higher speed than checks of the data use of skills. A check before installation can become a gate.
Why it made the cut
For teams that let staff install agent skills: make a list of the skills with access to files and accounts, and examine the ones that use personal data first.

# Privacy audit flags over half of AI agent skills handling personal data
A static check of 563 public AI assistant add-ons found that 307 may use people's data beyond what their descriptions say. It also flagged skills that NVIDIA's security scanner had already passed. The study is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

The authors built a tool, SkillPrivus, that reads a skill's code and instruction files without running it. It breaks the skill into individual data operations, such as reading, saving, sending or inferring information. Each operation is pinned to the exact line of source it comes from.

The authors collected 726 skills from public marketplaces, including ClawHub and SkillsMP, plus Anthropic's and NVIDIA's official collections. After setting aside skills with no personal data and some that failed analysis, 563 remained. The tool, run on the open-weight model gpt-oss-120b, flagged at least one potential violation in 307 of them, about 55%.

## The study
